newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean LG Semicon to boost non-memory chip sales.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean LG Semicon to boost non-memory chip sales.

text.p: South Korea's LG Semicon Co Ltd unveiled an ambitious plan on Monday to become one of the world's top five suppliers of non-memory chips.

Unlike memory chips mainly used for storing data, non-memory chips perform much more complicated tasks. They range from application-specific integrated circuits to digital signal processors and microprocessors.
LG Semicon, a unit of LG Group and one of the nation's top three chip makers, said it aimed to raise sales of non-memory chips to 30 percent of its overall sales by 2005 from 11 percent in 1995.
It estimated annual sales would rise to 30 trillion won ($36.45 billion) by 2005 compared with 2.5 trillion won in 1995, LG's executive director Kim Nak-ju told a news conference.
Mun Chung-hwan, the company's Chief Executive Officer, said: "World demand for non-memory chips will grow rapidly. So we must focus more on the area."
Analysts said the timing of the announcement appeared designed to fan interest in the company's initial public offering this week.
The Seoul stock market is currently in the doldrums.
LG Semicon, 54 percent owned by LG Electronics Inc, plans to offer 10 million shares at 20,000 won per share on Wednesday and Thursday. It initially planned to price the issue at 23,000 won.
"There is little new in the announcement," said an analyst at a local securities firm.
"Basically, it's aimed at the share offering," said the analyst, who asked not to be identified.
Officials at lead manager Hyundai Securities say they are confident the offer would be easily oversubscribed. The stock market has dropped 20.8 percent since this year's peak in May.
Alarmed by plunging international prices for memory chips as a result of a global oversupply, South Korean chipmakers are hurriedly trying to switch to non-memory chips, which have higher value.
Samsung Electronics Co and Hyundai Electronics Industries Co also have announced plans to expand non-memory chip production.
International spot prices for 16-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips have fallen to around $10 per unit from $45 to $50 this time last year.
LG's Mun said it was unlikely memory chip prices would recover this year. "We have several scenarios on price trends and the best case is that there will be no turnaround."

Mun also said his company was still committed to setting up a memory chip joint venture in Malaysia with Hitachi Ltd despite market speculation that the $1.25 billion deal may be aborted due to the industry's woes.
He said the project had been delayed "due to prolonged negotiations with the Malaysian government on details".
LG and Toshiba said early this year the joint venture would have the capacity to process 30,000 eight-inch wafers a month andconstruction would begin in the first half of this year.
